work_packages.name: A test effect that drifts with time moves by even steps at the display's refresh, between ticks and past the newest one
work_packages.quality_bar: Motion that is a function of time, shown as evenly as cloud shadows in Red Dead Redemption 2 or waves in Sea of Thieves on a 120 Hz display over a 60 Hz simulation: while the world's clock runs, equal steps of display time from frame to frame for equal intervals between consumed targets, no short step followed by a long one, no step when a tick commits, and no frame held on a tick while the world moves on. Display time is the world's time and never shows the time its clock was stopped: after a pause or an overload it goes on from the committed tick and does not go back, and it steps only where the design's table of a span's edges says, by no more than it says. Alpha stays the same function of the clock sample and the consumed target. A frame shows the tick it showed before WP4 wherever that tick was due by the frame's observation, which is every frame of an inline world. Only a delayed frame on a world on its own thread shows an earlier one.

items.statement: The world's clock gives the phase of a consumed target, which is an observation plus a lead: the fraction of the next tick elapsed at the observation plus the lead in ticks, with no stop at 1. It is never below 0 and never more than 50 ms of ticks above 1. While the clock is paused, overloaded, holding or has ticks queued it is exactly 1, and the clock's sample says it is not interpolating. The interpolation alpha for the same consumed target is unchanged bit for bit and is the phase held to 1. Sampling admits no tick and changes no clock. A world lane and a clocked world give their clock's phase.
items.ask: Are the expected phases written in the test from its scripted observations, tick rate and leads, and not computed with the clock's own phase function? Do they include a consumed target past the next tick's due time, one at the bound and one beyond it, a tick rate other than 60 Hz, and each state that gives exactly 1?

items.statement: An interpolating clock sample gives the due time of its tick: the host time at which the newest committed tick fell due. On a clock driven at scripted host times, from a start that is not host time zero on a world that is not on tick 0, through ticks that queue and then commit, a pause partway through a tick, a resume, an overload, and an overload with ticks still queued, at 60 Hz and at one other tick rate: a span begins at the start and at each resume, at host time R with the world on tick C_R, and tick C_R + k is due at R plus k tick durations, so the time the clock was stopped and the part-tick it discarded are in no span; queued ticks move no due time; a resume is refused while ticks are queued and holds until its first tick commits; and every interpolating frame under the phase's bound has a display time (its tick, less one, plus its phase, in tick durations) of the world time of the tick before its own plus its consumed target less its due time. Each holds to the precision the test states. A clocked world and a world lane give their clock sample's due time, and a world whose tick is rewound while its clock runs keeps the due time on the tick it lands on.
items.ask: Is every expected due time and display time worked out in the test from its scripted start, resume and observation times and the tick the world stood on, and never from a phase, an alpha or a due time the clock returned? Does the pause fall partway through a tick, so that a clock which kept the part-tick, or a test which left it out, would fail?

items.statement: A world on its own thread shows each poll a pair, a clock sample with the page committed with it: the newest whose clock is not interpolating or whose tick was due at or before the poll's observation, out of the pair the world has just published, the refused pair and the pair already shown. A published pair it cannot show becomes the refused pair. A delayed poll, one made after the world committed a tick due later than its observation, therefore shows an earlier tick than the world's newest, with a lead or without, and its phase and alpha are that pair's. No poll shows an earlier pair than one already shown. In a run of delayed polls, each observed on the running clock after the poll before it, every poll after the first shows a tick at least as new as the newest the poll before it saw. Each completed tick is counted once across the polls' reports, and the world's thread keeps committing throughout.
items.ask: Does the test make every poll of its run a delayed one, by waiting until the world has committed a tick due after the observation it then polls with? Would that run fail on a lane that holds only the pair it shows?

items.statement: A world on its own thread keeps one origin for each span. Started at host time zero on tick 0, paused and resumed through its lane's lifecycle requests while polls read each observation from the running clock, with and without a gap before the poll that is long enough for a tick to commit: every interpolating poll before the pause reports its tick's world time as the due time; every poll made while the world is paused or holding reports a clock that is not interpolating and a phase of exactly 1; the first interpolating poll after the resume shows a tick after the resume's; the due times of the interpolating polls after the resume, each less its tick's world time, agree; and the due time they give the resume's tick lies between the test's request for the resume and the reply it read. Each holds to the precision the test states.
items.ask: Does the test take its bracket from its own reads of the host clock before the request and after the reply, and each due time from the lane and not from a phase? Does at least one arm poll after a gap in which the world committed a tick?

items.statement: Each submitted frame gives every effect the display phase beside alpha, and the frame's completed sample reports it with the frame's tick, its observation, its lead, whether the clock was interpolating and, when it was, the due time of the frame's tick. In the V1 game with 60 Hz ticks, whose world starts at host time zero on tick 0, on a world that has not stopped: every interpolating frame under the phase's bound reports its tick's world time as the due time, and its display time (its tick, less one, plus its phase, in ticks) is its consumed target less one tick, to the precision the test states. That holds with leads from zero to 50 ms, at consumed targets 1/120 s apart and again 1/60 s apart, across a tick's commit, on frames whose alpha is 1 and more than one tick past the committed tick; for the inline world at scripted observations and for the world on its own thread; and for a delayed frame there with no lead, which shows an earlier tick than the world's newest, the one the effect and the completed sample both carry. In every frame alpha is the phase held to 1, and the diagnostic effect's state follows the state table as it did. A capture frame and a paused world give exactly 1 and report a clock that was not interpolating.
items.ask: Does the test work each frame's expected display time and due time out from its own observations and leads and the world's start, state the precision it holds them to, and read the phase from the effect time a contribution received? Is its delayed frame observed before a tick that the world has committed by the time the frame polls, so that the newest tick would fail it? Does any source that reads a clock, in the engine or the apps, form its phase from an alpha already held at 1, or fall back to one?

items.statement: Submitted frames of the V1 game keep the timing model through a stop. On the inline world at scripted host times, paused partway through a tick and resumed a second later, with leads of zero, 10 and 50 ms: every frame of the pause and of the hold gives a phase and an alpha of exactly 1 and reports a clock that was not interpolating; every interpolating frame after the resume reports the due time the script gives, the resume's time plus one tick duration for each tick since the resume's, and its display time is the world time of the tick before its own plus its consumed target less that due time; and the first of them shows a display time at or after the committed tick's world time, so neither the paused second nor the discarded part-tick is shown. On the world on its own thread, paused and resumed through its lifecycle requests, the frames after the resume report due times that give one origin and put the resume's tick between the test's request and the reply it read, and each has the display time its own record gives. Each holds to the precision the test states. In every frame the effect and the completed sample carry the same tick, phase and alpha.

items.statement: C02 in `docs/design/CONTRACTS.md` states the timing model as the design's section does: host time and world time kept apart; spans, and what begins and ends one; the due time of a frame's tick, and that an interpolating frame's record carries it; the phase, its bound and that alpha is the phase held to 1; display time, and that it holds no stopped time; that sampling never advances authority; that an interpolating frame's tick was due at or before its observation, so a world on its own thread shows a delayed frame an earlier pair and holds the refused pair for a later poll; that a host measures the lead from the observation where one clock gives both; and that a quantity shown past the committed tick is a presentation-only prediction from committed state, carried a tick at a time by its own step. `docs/EFFECTS.md` says the same to an effect's author. work_packages.name: A game's question to an effect is answered every tick from the state the last drawn frame left, even when that tick's frame is skipped, on the Mac and in Chrome
work_packages.quality_bar: A query path as in Unity's Crest ocean queries and Unreal's GPU readbacks: asked by the simulation's step, answered a step or two later without a stall, and no later when the renderer drops a frame. A wrong declaration is refused when the scene is prepared, with a named error, and never becomes a wrong answer.

items.statement: A contribution declares tick passes beside its frame passes, and preparation holds the stage's rules. It accepts a tick pass that reads its effect's persistent resources and reads its histories by `previous`. It refuses each of these with a named error: a tick pass that reads a history by `next`; one that reads a history by `result`; a tick pass that writes a transient, persistent or history resource or an attachment; a tick pass that reads a transient or an attachment; and a tick pass declared in a 2D scene. Guard: CPU tests of the declaration checks in `thrum-render`.

On Metal a test effect's tick pass answers from the state the last submitted frame left, whether or not a view is drawn, and each answer is delivered at a drain that needs no view. The effect keeps an integer field that each submitted frame steps. The test is its game: it posts points, each with the world endpoint it is asked on and the tick its answer is for, the tick pass reads the field at them, and the test drains the answers. In one scripted run the drained answers equal a CPU oracle of the field exactly in each of these advances: one that also submits a view, where the answer is the state before that view; one that finds every frame slot held; one whose host has a presenter and is given no drawable; one whose admitted frame is dropped before it is recorded; and the advance after a view was recorded and discarded. In the three advances that submit no view the answer is drained with no view submitted between its post and that drain, and the host's count of dropped views rises as it does today. In an advance that completes two ticks, with a point posted on each at different places, capacity for both and neither expired, the host makes one tick submission and two answers are drained, each carrying its own use tick and each the oracle's value at its own point. An advance with nothing posted makes no submission. Declaring the tick pass leaves the scene's compiled frame graph as it was, in its passes and its storage. Guard: a small Metal test in `thrum-render`, since only a device shows what a submission executes and when its readback maps.
items.ask: Are the expected values worked out by a CPU oracle of the field and never read from the engine? In the advances that submit no view, would the test fail if the tick pass were recorded with the next view, or if its answer reached the drain only after the next view? In the advance of two ticks, would the test fail if only the newer tick's post were answered? Is the frame host the only code that submits a tick pass's encoder, with a contribution given no device or queue submission of its own?

items.statement: A tick submission is bounded, needs its caller's permission, follows the device's lifecycle and is timed. On Metal, with the test effect of WP6.2: at the host's declared bound of outstanding tick submissions, an advance with work posted records none, counts one tick submission refused at the bound and returns without waiting, and a later advance submits the work once a submission has completed. With a submission permission that refuses, as a revoked lease does, an advance with work posted makes no tick submission, leaves the work posted and counts one tick submission refused for want of permission, in a count apart from the bound's. With a permission that grants, on a host that has a presenter and is given no drawable, the tick submission is made and its answer is drained, and the permission is entered before that submission's first queue call and left after its submit returns, as a test permission that records both observes. `advance_without_rendering` with work posted makes no tick submission and leaves the work posted. A capture runs no tick pass. After device replacement a result outstanding on the old generation is never delivered. With timing requested, an advance that makes a tick submission and submits a view reports the tick pass's GPU time under its own name, and with the switch off the pass writes no timestamp. Guard: a small Metal test in `thrum-render`, since only a device shows a submission's completion, a replaced generation and a timestamp.
items.ask: Is there no blocking poll and no blocking map between a post and its drain? Is there any path on which the frame host makes a tick submission's queue call outside the permission it was given? Does the tick stage create no timestamp query set of its own? Do the tests that hold `advance_without_rendering` to touching no device still stand as they were?

items.statement: In Chrome the V1 game's diagnostic effect has a tick pass that reads its trail field at posted points, and the game drains its answers with no view drawn. The drained answers equal the CPU oracle exactly in three cases: in advances that submit a view; for a point posted in an advance whose admitted frame is dropped before it is recorded, drained while the case goes on dropping every frame, with the host's count of submitted views at that drain equal to its count at the post; and on the replacement device after a device loss and recovery, for a point posted once a view has been submitted there. Guard: one browser case, since only Chrome shows that a submission and a map outside the frame complete on WebGPU and reach a drain through the browser's event loop.

An answer never comes from another world's state. On Metal, with the test effect of WP6.2, after a frame has committed the field, in each of three changes: the world restores onto another timeline at the same tick; a new world epoch reuses the tick and the timeline; and the device is replaced. A point posted on the changed world, and asked for before any view of it has been submitted, is drained carrying its post's endpoint and the mark of an answer made with no state, and holds no value of the field. In the first two changes the point is one where the committed field and the reset field differ, so an answer read from the old state would show. Once a view of the changed world has been submitted, a point posted there is drained with the oracle's value of the re-seeded field and without the mark. Guard: a small Metal test in `thrum-render`, since only a device shows what a submission read.

On the Mac a posted tick pass does not wait for a frame slot. With its surface ready and every frame slot held, the render actor makes the host's asking before the first poll or sleep of its wait for a slot, and it has made it whether a slot frees before the deadline or none does. Guard: a CPU test of the render actor's wait in `thrum-app` against a stand-in for the host that records the order of its calls, since the order is the claim and no panel timing is.
items.ask: In `crates/thrum-app/src/app/render_actor.rs`, is there any path on which the render actor polls or sleeps for a frame slot before the host's asking has been made? Does the tested wait run in the render actor's frame path, and not only in the test? Are the wait's deadline, the lead it measures afterwards and the `advance` that follows unchanged?

items.statement: The iPhone's render owner gives the frame host a submission permission made of its surface lease. Run against the lease with a stand-in surface, the permission runs the submission it is given while a surface is installed under the current epoch and the app is in the foreground. It refuses, and runs nothing, in each of three states: no surface installed; the lease revoked; and the background flag set. A removal of the surface attempted while the submission runs finds the lease busy until the submission returns. Guard: CPU tests beside the lease's own in `v1-game-ios`, which run on the Mac.
items.ask: Does every host the iPhone's render owner drives hold this permission from before its first advance, and keep it through a device recovery? Is each of the render owner's calls to `advance` and `drive` outside every lease section, so the permission's section cannot nest? Is the tested permission the one the render owner gives the host?
